title: The 25 August BAS Bill: Why Extra Time to Lodge Isn't Extra Cash to Spend
linkedin:
If your BAS is lodged through a registered tax agent, the April to June quarter isn't due until 25 August. That extra five weeks feels like breathing room after EOFY.

It isn't extra cash. It's a deferred bill with the due date moved, not the liability.

The GST sitting in the account right now was collected from customers across April, May and June. By the time the bill lands in late August, that quarter feels finished, the next one is well underway, and the money has usually already gone into wages, stock, or a supplier payment that couldn't wait.

Here's the part that catches people out. It's rarely that owners misjudge the size of the number. Most can estimate it within a reasonable margin. What catches them out is that the account balance by late August reflects momentum from the new quarter's trading, not the liability that was actually locked in back in June. The bill lands right when the business feels furthest from the quarter that generated it.

Businesses that self-lodge and pay by 28 July rarely hit this problem, because the gap between collecting the GST and paying it stays inside one quarter's trading rhythm. The concession that helps a tax agent manage their workload quietly removes that alignment for everyone lodging through them, unless the business rebuilds the discipline itself.

The fix is unglamorous. Treat GST as money that was never yours from the moment it lands, not the week before it's due. A weekly or fortnightly transfer of the GST component into a separate account does more to prevent a August cash shock than any amount of after the fact budgeting.

A note for East Coast business owners who lodge their BAS through a registered tax agent. The April to June quarter carries a concessional due date of 25 August, a full five weeks later than the 28 July deadline that applies to businesses lodging themselves.

That extra time is genuinely useful for managing paperwork with your agent. It is not extra cash. The GST sitting in the account this week was collected from customers over April, May and June, and it was never really the business's money to begin with.

The pattern we see most often is that by the time the bill is actually due, trading has moved well into the new quarter. The account balance reflects that new momentum, not the liability that was locked in back in June, so the payment can feel like a bigger hit than it should.

A simple habit fixes most of this. Set the GST component aside into a separate account as it's collected, on a weekly or fortnightly rhythm, rather than waiting for the BAS deadline to work out what's owed. It turns a quarterly scramble into something routine.

If your BAS bill landed heavier than expected this year, it's worth understanding why before the next quarter closes. Read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.
